newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-OWNERS RATIFY 5-YR AGREEMENT WITH PLAYERS.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-OWNERS RATIFY 5-YR AGREEMENT WITH PLAYERS.

text.p: Baseball owners on Tuesday ratified a new five-year labour agreement in an effort to end years of turmoil with the players' union that caused a bitter strike and cancelled the 1994 World Series.
The vote was 26-4 in favour of the agreement, three more than the three-quarters majority needed. It still must be approved by the Major League Players Association.
"We can now live together and bring peace to the game," said interim baseball commissioner Bud Selig. "The difficult times are now behind us."

Under the agreement, there will be inter-league play in 1997, teams with high payrolls will pay a so-called "luxury tax," and that money will be paid in part to poorer teams playing in smaller markets.
"The problems we have endured have come to a conclusion," Selig said. "It is now time for us to move forward, put everything else behind us."

The vote on Tuesday was a major switch from the owners' first vote taken earlier this month. Then, the deal reached in August by owners' negotiator Randy Levine and union chief Don Fehr was rejected by an 18-12 vote.

But when Jerry Reinsdorf of the Chicago White Sox, the leader of the group most actively against the agreement, signed Cleveland slugger Albert Belle to a five-year $55 million contract, the other owners rebelled and demanded a new vote.
The Major League Players Association, which conducted a strike against the owners between August 1994 and April 1995, have a meeting scheduled next week in Puerto Rico.
Selig noted, "This was a long and difficult process. It passed by three votes. It was time to get this behind us and move baseball forward."

The agreement, if ratified by the players, means that financially distressed, small-market franchises such as Montreal and Pittsburgh will receive an infusion of needed capital that may enable them to get through next season.

The flip side of the coin shows that the players will regain 75 days of service time lost during the strike, which may make some Montreal players eligible for free agency and therefore too expensive for the Expos.
Chicago will lose ace right-hander Alex Fernandez to free agency, but have vowed to spend the money to resign him.
The luxury tax, which will begin next year and run for three years, will be paid by teams with a payroll above $51 million next year, going up to $59 million in the final year.
Interleague play between American and National League teams will start next year, with the revised schedule to be released around Christmas.
During interleague play, World Series rules will prevail, with a designated hitter being used in American League stadiums.
The club owners will be granted the right by players to expand by two more clubs.
In addition the minimum major league salary will rise from $109,000 this year to $150,000 next year, $170,000 in 1998 and $200,000 after that.
